procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated July 27, 1964 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 481 of 1963, dismissing Jamuna Singh's appeal and confirming his conviction and sentence under ss. 323 and 436 read with s. 109, I. P. C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Four individuals, including Jamuna Singh and Jodha Singh, appealed their convictions to the Patna High Court. The High Court acquitted two of the appellants. It acquitted Jodha Singh of the offence under s. 436 I.P.C. but maintained his conviction under s. 323 I.P.C. Jamuna Singh's appeal was dismissed, upholding his convictions under sections 323 and 436 read with 109 of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Jamuna Singh appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the Patna High Court's decision to uphold his conviction.

decision.conviction_status: The conviction under s. 323 I.P.C. is upheld. The conviction under s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C. is altered to one under s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C.
decision.sentence_status: Reduced to four years' rigorous imprisonment.

issue.issue_text: Whether a person can be convicted of abetting an offence when the person alleged to have committed the main offence in consequence of the abetment has been acquitted.

law.description: Defines abetment as occurring in one of three ways: (1) instigating a person to do an act, (2) engaging in a conspiracy with others to do an act, or (3) intentionally aiding the doing of an act.
Clarifies that for the offence of abetment to be constituted, it is not necessary that the abetted act actually be committed.
Provide for the punishment of abetment even if the main offence is not committed as a consequence of the abetment.

application.description: The Court first established that there is no absolute rule in law stating an abettor must be acquitted if the principal offender is. The abettor's guilt depends on the specific nature and manner of the abetment.

The Court analyzed the three types of abetment under Section 107 I.P.C. It distinguished between abetment by 'instigation' or 'conspiracy' on one hand, and abetment by 'intentionally aiding' on the other.

For abetment by 'instigation' or 'conspiracy', the Court held that the offence of abetment is complete at the moment of instigation or when the conspiracy is formed. Citing Sections 108, 115, and 116, it reasoned that since the main offence does not need to be committed for the abetment to be a crime, the acquittal of the person who was supposed to commit the act is irrelevant to the abettor's guilt.

Conversely, for abetment by 'intentionally aiding', the Court stated that the charge against the abettor is directly linked to the commission of the main offence. If the principal offender is acquitted, it implies the main offence was not committed. In such a case, a person cannot be held guilty of 'aiding' an offence that never happened. Therefore, a charge of abetment by aiding would be expected to fail.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the proposition that an abettor can never be convicted when the principal offender is acquitted. The outcome depends on the type of abetment. If the abetment was by instigation or conspiracy, the abettor can still be convicted as the offence of abetment is independent of the commission of the main crime. However, if the abetment was by intentionally aiding the commission of the offence, the abettor's charge would likely fail upon the acquittal of the principal offender.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 of the Indian Penal Code when the person charged with the main offence was acquitted and there was no finding that the offence was committed by any other person at the appellant's instigation.

facts: The appellant was convicted for abetting (under s. 109 IPC) a co-accused, Jodha Singh, to commit mischief by fire (under s. 436 IPC).
The High Court acquitted the co-accused, Jodha Singh, of the main offence of setting the fire.
Despite acquitting the main offender, the High Court maintained the appellant's conviction for abetment.
There was no finding by the lower courts that any other person had set the fire at the appellant's instigation.
law: A conviction for abetment under s. 109 of the Indian Penal Code requires that the abetted act is committed *in consequence of the abetment*.

The Court clarified that it is not an absolute rule that an abettor cannot be convicted when the main offender is acquitted; the abettor's guilt depends on the specific facts and the nature of the abetment.
application: The Court applied the law to the facts by noting that the person who was allegedly instigated, Jodha Singh, had been acquitted. This meant the court found that he did not commit the act of setting the fire.
Since there was also no evidence or finding that anyone else set the fire as a consequence of the appellant's instigation, a crucial element for a conviction under s. 109 was missing.
The act of setting fire (the s. 436 offence) was not proven to have occurred as a consequence of the appellant's abetment.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellant could not be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 of the IPC. This was because the person he allegedly instigated was acquitted of the main offence, and there was no finding that the offence was committed by any other person as a consequence of the appellant's instigation.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant, having been found to have instigated the commission of an offence under s. 436 I.P.C., could be convicted under s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C. instead.

facts: The appellant was initially convicted under s. 436 read with s. 109 of the Indian Penal Code (I.P.C.) for instigating a co-accused, Jodha Singh, to burn a hut.
The co-accused, Jodha Singh, who was alleged to have set the fire, was acquitted by the High Court of the offence under s. 436.
Despite acquitting the main offender, the High Court maintained the appellant's conviction for abetment under s. 436 read with s. 109.
The appellant argued before the Supreme Court that his conviction for abetment was illegal since the person he allegedly instigated had been found not guilty.
The High Court had found as a fact that the appellant did instigate the co-accused to commit the offence.
law: Section 109 I.P.C. applies to the abetment of an offence when the offence is actually committed in consequence of that abetment.
Section 115 I.P.C. applies when an offence punishable with life imprisonment (such as an offence under s. 436) is abetted, but the offence is not committed in consequence of the abetment.

The court held that an abettor can be convicted even if the person alleged to have committed the main offence is acquitted. The abettor's guilt depends on the nature of the act abetted and the manner of abetment (e.g., instigation).
A person who instigates another to commit an offence is guilty of abetment under s. 115 or s. 116 I.P.C., even if the offence is not ultimately committed.
application: The Court determined that the appellant's conviction under s. 436 read with s. 109 was incorrect. This was because s. 109 requires the abetted act to be committed as a consequence of the instigation, but the person instigated (Jodha Singh) was acquitted.
Although the hut was set on fire by someone, there was no finding that this was done as a consequence of the appellant's instigation. Therefore, the condition for s. 109 was not met.
However, the High Court had established that the appellant did instigate Jodha Singh to commit the offence under s. 436. This act of instigation itself constitutes the offence of abetment.
Since the offence abetted (under s. 436) is punishable with life imprisonment and was not committed in consequence of the instigation, the correct legal provision to apply was s. 115 I.P.C.
The Court found that it could legally alter the conviction to the lesser offence under s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C. and reduced the sentence accordingly.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument in part. It held that since the instigated person was acquitted and the offence was not committed as a consequence of the abetment, a conviction under s. 109 I.P.C. was improper. However, because the appellant was proven to have instigated the crime, he was still guilty of abetment. The Court, therefore, altered the conviction from s. 436 read with s. 109 I.P.C. to s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C. and reduced the sentence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person can be convicted of abetting an offence when the person alleged to have committed the main offence in consequence of the abetment has been acquitted.
appellant_arguments: The conviction for abetment is bad in law when the person who is said to have committed the main offence at the instigation of the abettor has been held to be not guilty.
If the principal offender is acquitted and the main offence is held not to have been committed, then no question of intentionally aiding the commission of that offence arises.
respondent_arguments: An abettor can be convicted even if the named principal offender is acquitted, provided the court finds that the criminal act was committed by some person as a consequence of the abetment. (Inferred from the court's finding)

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant could be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 of the Indian Penal Code when the person charged with the main offence was acquitted and there was no finding that the offence was committed by any other person at the appellant's instigation.
appellant_arguments: The appellant could not be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 109 because the person charged with the main offence (Jodha Singh) had been acquitted, and there was no finding by the lower courts that the fire was set by any other person participating in the incident at the appellant's instigation.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's decision to confirm the conviction under s. 436 read with s. 109 should be upheld. (Inferred, as the respondent would be defending the lower court's judgment)

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant, having been found to have instigated the commission of an offence under s. 436 I.P.C., could be convicted under s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C. instead.
appellant_arguments: The appellant sought a reduction in sentence, noting that the punishment for an offence under s. 436 read with s. 115 is less severe than that under s. 436 read with s. 109. (Implicit argument for a lesser charge)
respondent_arguments: If the conviction under s. 109 cannot be sustained, the appellant should still be convicted under s. 115 based on the established fact that he instigated the offence. (Inferred)

cases.case_name: Barendra Kumar Ghosh v. The King Emperor
cases.principle: Cited in support of the principle that a conviction for abetment under s. 109 IPC is not sustainable when the principal offender has been acquitted and there is no finding that the offence was committed by any other person at the instigation of the appellant.

cases.case_name: Faguna Kanta Nath v. The State of Assam
cases.principle: Cited to support the legal position that a conviction for abetment under s. 109 IPC is incorrect in law when the person charged with the main offence has been acquitted and there is no finding that the act was committed by any other person at the instigation of the abettor.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction for abetment under Section 109 of the Indian Penal Code is incorrect in law if the person charged with the main offense has been acquitted and there is no finding that the offense was committed by any other person in consequence of the abettor's instigation. In such a scenario, if the act of instigation is proven, the conviction should be under Section 115 of the Indian Penal Code for abetment of an offense that was not committed.
obiter: In a previous case, it was held that where a person sets fire to a hut as a member of an unlawful assembly, it is considered to be in consequence of the abettor's order, and it would be unreal to hold that the act was done independently of the instigation.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A conviction for abetment where the abetted act is committed (s. 109 I.P.C.) cannot be sustained when the person charged with the main offence has been acquitted, and there is no specific finding by the courts that the offence was actually committed by any other person as a consequence of the abetment. While the act of instigation is proven, the conviction must be altered to abetment where the offence is not committed (s. 115 I.P.C.), as the commission of the principal crime itself has not been legally established.
legal_tests_applied: To convict an individual for abetment under s. 109 I.P.C. (where the act is committed), it is necessary to have a judicial finding that the principal offence was in fact committed by some person as a consequence of the abetment. The acquittal of a specifically named principal offender is not an absolute bar, but the commission of the act itself by an identifiable person or a member of a group must be established as a matter of fact.
why_appellant_lost: The Supreme Court accepted the High Court's finding of fact that the appellant had instigated his co-accused to commit the offence under s. 436 I.P.C. This established the act of abetment, making him liable for punishment, even if the main offence was not proven to have been committed as a result. As the court states: 'It had been held by the High Court that the appellant had instigated his co-accused to commit the offence. under s. 436 I.P.C. He must therefore be held guilty under s. 436 read with s. 115 I.P.C.'
why_respondent_won: The respondent succeeded in maintaining a conviction for abetment because the court upheld the factual finding that the appellant had instigated the crime. The legal argument that abetment requires a successful commission of the main crime for any conviction to stand was rejected; the court simply shifted the conviction to a section of the penal code that punishes instigation even if the instigated act does not occur.
policy_considerations: A conviction must be based on a specific finding of fact, not on an assumption that because an act was instigated, it must have been carried out by someone. The court distinguished this case from a prior one where it was considered a realistic finding that someone in an unlawful assembly must have committed the act, noting that in this case, such a finding was absent. This implies a policy against convictions that are 'unreal and completely divorced from the facts of the case.'
